I think what you're really asking is "what is the difference between the current Democratic Party platform and the 'God-given rights' the Founders assumed we all had, as stated in our founding documents?"

My answer would be that the current Democratic Party platform focuses on equity, rather than equality. It may use the word "equality," but it really means equity, which is focused on"equal outcome," rather than the simple principle of "equal opportunity" that was established during the Enlightenment by thinkers such as John Locke (whose philosophy had a very strong influence on Thomas Jefferson, the most prominent, and possibly the sole, writer of the final version of the Constitution).

An "equity" policy is essentially a policy that attempts to help historically oppressed groups (such as American blacks, Native Americans, women, etc.) succeed more readily in the U.S. by making it easier for them to get into college, get hired, and receive federal, state, and local financial support in the form of tax redistribution. It does this through a vast network of federal, state, and local regulations and programs. Democrats will often argue that the "God-given rights" of life, liberty, and property require such policies, especially since, in the race to success, these historically oppressed groups are "starting far behind" those who have classically held the reins of power, namely American whites. This argument, of course, has many flaws (mostly, IMHO, having to do with what sociologists call "latent dysfunctions" in the form of the practical effects such policies have on both the individuals they are trying to help and on society at large).

But I won't go into those in detail here. I will simply say that while one could argue that both the current Republican Party platform and the current Democratic Party platform are supportive of the Constitution and advocate the rights contained therein, it is pretty difficult to argue that rights that the government has over your life in the form of the policy of both major parties is close to what the Founders intended. Additionally, it is quite a stretch to find support for the surveillance state, constant overseas warfare, the extremely bloated and inefficient federal welfare state, and significant corporate federal subsidy schemes with anything in the Constitution.
